# Likely judge questions, with honest answers

*Generated by `presentation/build.py` from `artifacts/*.json`. Numbers update when the experiments are re-run.*

## Is this the first time-crystal quantum reservoir?
No. Zhang et al. (arXiv:2508.15230, 2025) used essentially the same model (imperfect π kicks, random ZZ and Z fields, reset-and-inject input, ⟨Z⟩/⟨ZZ⟩ readout) on synthetic tasks and found phase boundaries best. Our work is an independent replication and extension. We add real time series, classical baselines matched in feature count and readout, a check of whether the best-memory phase also forecasts best, and the measurement cost. See `docs/literature.md`.

## Do you claim quantum advantage?
No. Linear AR is the best forecaster on both series, with test NMSE 0.131 on sunspots and 0.112 on CO2. The quantum reservoir's medians are 0.381 and 0.205. It beats AR on 0 of 8 seeds on sunspots and 0 of 8 on CO2.

## Did you run on quantum hardware?
No. Everything is exact NumPy density-matrix simulation of 6 qubits on a laptop. One reservoir step is cross-checked against Qiskit Aer's density-matrix simulator in `tests/`. Shot noise and depolarizing noise are simulated.

## Why is the time crystal bad at memory, when it is "robust"?
Its robustness is robustness to perturbations, and the input is a perturbation. Near θ = π the chain mostly flips back and forth; the injected state on qubit 0 barely spreads. At θ = 0.95π the period-doubling order is 0.97 and memory capacity is 1.32. Across the scan, memory capacity and time-crystal order correlate at r = -0.51.

## Is the comparison fair to the quantum model?
We tried to make it so. Every model sees the same scaled series and the same time-ordered splits. The series is min–max scaled on the training block only, not clipped, and a test checks this. The quantum reservoir and ESN both give 11 features to the same ridge readout. AR uses at most 11 lags. θ, ridge α, ESN spectral radius and input scale, and AR order are all chosen on validation only. Models are refitted on train + validation and tested once. The quantum model gets 6 kick angles to choose from; the ESN gets a comparable small grid of spectral radius × input scale.

## Is a single split enough?
Yes. We also ran rolling-origin cross-validation, where each fold re-tunes every model on its own preceding validation block: sunspots, 4 folds: mean-rank order AR > ESN > Quantum reservoir > Persistence > J = 0 control; quantum reservoir mean rank 3.5 of 5, best in 0 of 4 folds; CO2, 4 folds: mean-rank order AR > ESN > Quantum reservoir > J = 0 control > Persistence; quantum reservoir mean rank 3 of 5, best in 0 of 4 folds. Rolling-origin cross-validation (4 folds) keeps the AR > ESN > quantum order on both series by mean rank. In those folds the quantum reservoir beats persistence on sunspots in median (0.26 vs 0.41) but is worse in 1 of 4 folds.

## Why does the phase chosen on validation not win on sunspots?
Sunspots have only 309 yearly values, so validation is 47 points: one or two solar cycles. Median validation NMSE is lowest at θ = 0.65π, but median test NMSE is lowest at θ = 0.95π, the time-crystal side that behaves like persistence. Per-seed choices were 0.5π ×2, 0.65π ×4, 0.8π ×2. We report this rather than picking θ on test.

## Why include a J = 0 control?
Without interactions, information cannot leave the input qubit, so it is a "quantum but trivial" reservoir. It isolates the contribution of many-body dynamics. On CO2 the interacting reservoir's median NMSE is 0.21 against 0.49 for J = 0. Its memory capacity stays at 0.57–1.07 at every θ.

## What does it cost on real hardware?
Two things. Shot noise: at θ = 0.5π memory capacity goes 5.17 → 4.27 → 2.64 → 1.33 from exact readout down to 100 shots. Restarts: projective measurement destroys the state, so the input sequence must be re-run up to each readout. That is 95,790 Floquet cycles per shot for the 309-step sunspot series instead of 618, and about 40 million circuit runs for our full forecasting protocol at 1,000 shots. Mujal et al. (2023) show windowed replay or weak measurement can reduce this.

## Why only 6 qubits?
Exact density matrices for 6 qubits are 64 × 64, which keeps the full scan (600 reservoir runs) and the forecasting grid at about 90 s on a laptop, with no shot noise unless we add it. Larger chains would add memory but also cost; we did not test them.

## What would make the quantum reservoir win?
A task that needs nonlinear memory beyond what AR captures, longer chains with more memory, and a readout protocol that does not destroy the state each step. Our benchmark is built so these can be tested with the same fair splits.

## How do you know the code is right?
`tests/` has 10 tests: the density matrix stays physical with and without noise; the Floquet operator is unitary; reset writes the input on qubit 0; a perfect π flip carries no input beyond qubit 0; one step matches Qiskit Aer's density-matrix simulator; shots converge to exact; capacity sanity checks; splits are time-ordered and scaling uses train only; the Diebold–Mariano sign convention.

## What is reusable for the community?
`qreservoir` is a small MIT-licensed package: an exact density-matrix Floquet reservoir with shots and noise, a matched ESN, memory-capacity and forecasting harnesses with validation-only tuning and Diebold–Mariano tests, and this generated deck. Swapping in another series or reservoir is a few lines.
